1.caption: Research Scope and Progression
rows: Develop a structured and evaluable representation of patient consent as a trust-aware authorisation object that explicitly connects identity, authority requirements, policy constraints, and authorisation evidence.
RO2: Decentralised Identity and Authority Trust
Establish trustworthy participants using decentralised identifiers and verifiable credentials while explicitly separating identity authentication from authorisation authority.
Establish collective trust by requiring multiple independently verified participants to satisfy predefined authorisation conditions before sensitive healthcare data access can be granted.
RO4: Policy- and Context-Aware Access Control

Ensure that authorised access remains consistent with the purpose, policy, and healthcare data scope specified by the consent, preventing valid identities and approvals from being used to obtain data beyond the authorised constraints.
Extend the authorisation model with validity periods, expiration, revocation, and controlled consent-state transitions to support dynamic and lifecycle-aware trust evaluation.
RO6: Formal Security Assurance and Empirical Validation

Formally define and analyse the security and authorisation properties of the proposed framework and empirically evaluate the complete HALAH implementation using representative healthcare data-sharing, negative, and adversarial scenarios.

3.caption: Descriptions, issues and limitations of existing studies on consent representation and blockchain-based consent governance
rows: The authentication and authorisation module of the iAgree patient-controlled data-sharing portal, deployed at three health systems, with OAuth2, SMART on FHIR and one-time-password identity, a patient preference matrix of data category by recipient type, and a permissioned Ethereum audit contract.

A single patient decides and multi-institution is not multi-party; authorisation is OAuth2 delegation with no separate authority evidence for researchers; enforcement of the preference matrix is out of scope; the one-hour window is a session token, not consent validity; revocation is append-only and untested; no formal methods; functional tests only.

Mainzelliste, an open-source pseudonymisation, record-linkage and consent-management service in production since 2015, with multi-tenant role-based access control, per-request token validation, modular FHIR consent directives scoped by use type, an automated consent-check capability and registry-level consent withdrawal.

The consent-check semantics, term list and allow or deny protocol are not specified in the paper; withdrawal is a registry operation whose downstream enforcement is not shown; no temporal validity; the secure multi-party computation parties perform record linkage, not authorisation; security evidence is a penetration test without formal analysis; no consent decision is verified.

4.caption: Descriptions, issues and limitations of existing studies on decentralised identity and authority trust
rows: A simulated Norwegian cross-institution exchange with EUDI-compatible wallets, W3C DIDs and VCs, an executable on-chain consent object (patient DID, requester DID, scope, expiry, state) on Hyperledger Besu, Groth16 access proofs, licensing-body credentials asserting role and scope of practice, run-time revocation (1.45 s) and an openEHR to FHIR bridge; allow and deny outcomes tested over 100 runs.

A single patient grants a bilateral agreement with no multi-party approval; the expiry field is stored but the access algorithm checks only state and proof; purpose is at the user-interface level with no policy engine; no threat model, formal verification or adversarial test; simulation only with a node-count inconsistency.

A design-only architecture for dynamic and auditable consent in secondary use in which a FHIR Consent resource carrying purpose, scope, actors and validity period is anchored on an Ethereum-compatible ledger, requester credentials are validated in three steps at a gateway, and validation of purpose, scope and duration at decision time is specified.

Explicitly not implemented and not evaluated, so no dimension is enforced; proxy or guardian delegation is a substitution option rather than joint approval; revocation is specified but not implemented; the STRIDE-style threat table is declared non-exhaustive with no proof or verification; same author group as [58].

EMR-Chain, an open-source decentralised record exchange combining an Ethereum identity chain, on which a government-endorsed hashed national identity is bound to a wallet, with a Hyperledger Fabric record chain using X.509 identities from the ministry certificate authority, health-authority-granted roles, a patient-adjustable per-hospital access list and JWT validation, benchmarked against national exchange statistics.

The identifier is not a W3C DID; the patient and requester co-signature is bilateral authentication, not independent approval; purpose is logged but never evaluated and scope is hospital-level; JWT expiry is a session bound rather than consent validity; access-list revocation does not invalidate issued tokens; narrative security discussion only.

5.caption: Descriptions, issues and limitations of existing studies on multi-party authorisation and collaborative consent
rows: Nexa, a public Avalanche blockchain record system with a public prototype and a Synthea-derived dataset, in which each record key is protected by a Shamir (5, 3) threshold; clinical access combines the requester's share with two automated oracle shares released on the current on-chain role, revocation of roles is checked at each request, and an institutional M-of-N multi-signature for bulk access is proposed.

The threshold is over key custodians, not authorisers: a single authorisation locus with no human co-approval and the patient's share not required; the institutional multi-signature is outside the prototype; role-based only with no purpose, context or temporal term; no formal proof or tool; performance measured with no allow or deny or attack test; estimated competitor values.

Informed consent represented as a patient-driven policy IC = (U, O, OP, CON) with hash integrity and contextual conditions (time, date, day, location, network address, frequency) that an authorisation module conjoins with organisational and regulatory policies; a Solidity consent-management contract is deployed on the Goerli testnet.

The only multi-party element is a two-of-two multi-signature wallet in the test harness that gates consent registration, with unnamed members and no place in the model; no purpose term; lifecycle operations described but not specified; enforcement mechanisms explicitly not included; no measured result or allow or deny case; assumptions only, no security analysis.

Deployed electronic informed consent for rare disease genomics at three Swedish genomic medicine centres on a commercial platform: a minor's consent is valid only when all legal guardians sign, guardianship is verified in real time against the national Population Register, authentication uses the national electronic identity, and adoption is reported for 2,244 invited participants.

The guardian condition applies at consent registration, not to the access decision; the only decision-time touchpoint answers whether a valid consent exists, without purpose, scope or time; study-level broad consent with no policy; withdrawal effect not described; centralised research platform described in little technical detail; no formal or authorisation-correctness evidence; vendor conflict of interest declared.

A retrospective comparative case study of the Swedish and Finnish national patient portals in which guardian proxy access to a minor's record is gated jointly by a healthcare professional's capacity assessment and the minor's own consent, with register-verified guardianship and age windows whose enforcement is evidenced by no use within blocked windows and 95.8 per cent of capable minors consenting to disclosure.

The collective condition is documentation-time governance in centralised national systems rather than a decision-time predicate in a decentralised exchange; consent is not an evaluable object with its own scope or purpose; the study is observational and offers no security analysis or formal assurance.

A fully decentralised multi-party consent scheme on Ethereum in which incapacitated-path access requires regulatory-agency approvals and at least min(ceil(0.7g), 5) guardian approvals on one request, emergency access requires agency approval and hospital admission confirmation, attestation expiry is enforced inside the decision, and claims and guardians can be revoked; a testnet prototype with gas costs is reported.

On the normal path a single patient key authorises, so joint approval is a contingency fallback rather than a condition of every decision; guardians hold no key shares and the regulatory agency can decrypt alone, so the joint guarantee is contract-level only; no policy, purpose or data-category model; no formal analysis, dataset, attack test or allow or deny matrix.

MedXBlock, a permissioned Ethereum access-control system with an implemented hybrid attribute- and role-based policy engine evaluating a conjunctive deny-by-default predicate over a stateful policy store, an M-of-N multi-signature contract over registered doctors and administrators for high-sensitivity and cross-departmental requests, token expiry checked at access, and 100 instrumented transactions.

The threshold is institution-side, scoped to sensitive requests, bypassable by a single emergency officer and outside the grant predicate; patient consent is a boolean attribute, not an evaluable object with its own scope, validity or lifecycle; no purpose term; a threat table and an asserted safety property only; systems metrics with no executed authorisation, denial or attack test; gas figures internally inconsistent.

Personal health record sharing with multi-party pre-authorisation verification in which the patient appoints n verifiers and a threshold t; each verifier checks the patient-issued grant, its expiry and the revocation list before releasing a share of the decryption key, so that t validated shares are needed to obtain the record; the secure multi-party computation layer is implemented in Go on ten machines.

The joint approval is a pre-delegated contingency for an incapable patient; verifiers evaluate identity, grant, time and revocation but not purpose or data scope (attribute policy is future work); the identity, wallet, credential and ledger layers are not implemented; no authorisation test, no expired or revoked credential rejection test; STRIDE and LINDDUN enumeration with no proof over the protocol.

Soteria, a multi-site clinical-trial data platform on Hyperledger Fabric with trusted-execution chaincode in which a (t, n) threshold signature over named investigators gates the admission of trial records to the ledger and the revocation of a consent, consents carry enumerated states with start and end times and a study-number binding validated at an endpoint, and fourteen endpoints are timed on a managed deployment.

The consent grant is unilateral and the threshold governs record admission and revocation rather than the patient's access decision; each vote is a hash-integrity check by institution-side investigators; time is a stored attribute not shown to gate the decision; no policy engine; no theorem, proof or adversary model; performance only with borrowed latency figures and no correctness or attack evaluation.

6.caption: Descriptions, issues and limitations of existing studies on policy- and context-aware access control
rows: ConsentChain represents genomic-data consent as a machine-readable object of data type, role and purpose combined into an access-policy tree that is hashed and evaluated by a checkConsent function on a permissioned Ethereum network; the proof of concept is deployed with measured throughput and open source code.

Policy evaluation is a rigid hash exact-match rather than a policy engine; the requester role is self-submitted without credential verification; the consent tuple has no validity interval and time is enforced only at the delivery layer; revocation is a binary status; a single patient consents; the security analysis is qualitative and no adversarial or allow-and-deny suite is reported.

A consent model for blockchain-based health data sharing platforms in which the requester's purpose is matched inside the smart contract against the patient's consent through DUO and ADA-M ontology terms, with denial tested across several requester profiles.

Security assurance is explicitly outside the scope of the paper; the consent is granted by a single patient without guardian or threshold approval; temporal validity and lifecycle states are not enforced in the decision; identity and authority verification is only partially addressed.

A blockchain-based service-oriented architecture for consent management, access control and auditing in which FHIR Consent purpose-of-use limits are evaluated per resource by an XACML policy decision point over Hyperledger Fabric, with supervisory audit services.

No withdrawal or expiry path exists anywhere in the architecture; the authors state that the experiments validate the blockchain component only, so the authorisation decision is not verified; no multi-party approval, identity and authority only partially verified, and no formal security argument.

A purpose-based consent model for EHRs on Hyperledger Fabric in which consent is an evaluable tuple of role, doctor identifiers, action and intended purpose, matched by chaincode at request time against a purpose tree of allowed and prohibited purposes with per-datum scope.

The consent tuple has no temporal element; withdrawal is implemented but its effect on later access is untested and there is no state machine; identity relies on Fabric membership certificates without DIDs, VCs or authority credentials; consensus endorsement is not multi-party consent; no formal verification or threat model; the four-node prototype reports functional targets without quantitative results or attack cases.

7.caption: Descriptions, issues and limitations of existing studies on temporal validity and consent lifecycle
rows: EdgeConsent implements an on-chain attribute-based access control engine in which consent rules with not-before and not-after bounds, purposes, data categories, sensitivity levels and jurisdictions are evaluated by checkAccess against the requester attributes and the current timestamp, with deny-by-default; revocation is enforced at the next block and every decision is logged.

Lifecycle limited to an active flag and temporal bounds without pending, suspended or renewed states; wallet-address identity with unspecified attribute issuance and no DIDs or VCs; single-patient rules with no threshold; no threat model or formal properties; two-page demonstration on a local network with gas measurements but no adversarial or correctness suite.

A hybrid RBAC and smart-contract scheme with attribute-based authorisation for IoMT records in which the expiry of a signed credential is checked against the current time at every sharing interaction and authorisations are recorded on a grant ledger.

Time is enforced on the requester's credential rather than on the consent or authorisation object, which carries no validity window; no consent state machine; no multi-party approval; neither a formal proof of the authorisation decision nor decision-level correctness evidence is reported (both coded Partial).

A blockchain-enabled governance overlay for clinical AI pipelines in which a formal policy object with roles, purposes, a validity window, a revoked flag and a version is evaluated so that access is allowed only if the policy is valid at time t and the role and purpose hold; mid-stream revocation is verified at scale through a consent-drift metric, with denials ledgered and the artefact publicly archived.

Interval-bound denials are not separately exercised and the lifecycle is a binary active or revoked state; single-node hash-chain ledger without consensus; identity inherited from an existing clinical identity provider; single policy administrator with no multi-party approval; purpose is requester-declared set membership without attestation or scope; the authors declare that no formal verification was performed.

A patient-centric cryptographic protection scheme for cloud EHRs in which the patient's signed consent token, the requester role, the expiry time and delegation are inputs to key derivation, so that an expired or revoked consent makes the decryption key unreachable without re-encryption and role-scoped keys separate authority from identity.

No explicit lifecycle state machine; consent issued by a single patient key although the construction could accept a threshold; identity relies on a commercial authentication service and device keys without credentials; adversary model with a probabilistic statement but no proof or tool; only operation latency is measured, with literature values as baselines.

8.caption: Descriptions, issues and limitations of existing studies on formal security assurance and empirical validation
rows: A threshold traceable delegation authorisation scheme in which the data owner delegates to l of d already-authorised users, each running a private-key-bound authorisation algorithm before an out-of-policy requester can restore the data, with IND-CPA security reduced to the bilinear Diffie-Hellman assumption and unforgeability argued by reference.

Delegates are consumer-side clinicians rather than patient-side stakeholders and the owner's own decision is unilateral; identity is an escrowed identity-based key without authentication protocol or credentials; no purpose term and out-of-policy requesters bypass the policy by delegation; no time, expiry, revocation or states; accountability signature verifiable by the owner only; Java benchmark against the authors' own baseline with no system prototype or allow-and-deny tests.

A blockchain scheme for IoMT data of unconscious patients in which t of n patient-designated relatives contribute to threshold proxy re-encryption without the key being reassembled at any single point, the hospital and relatives are authenticated on chain through non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs, IND-CCA security is proven and a Solidity implementation is reported.

No policy, purpose or data-scope condition and no temporal validity in the decision; lifecycle limited to the emergency path without consent states; the proof covers the threshold and encryption predicate only; empirical validation is limited to an in-paper implementation (Req7 Partial) without a verified allow-and-deny suite.

A dual-revocation ciphertext-policy attribute-based encryption scheme for IoMT in which a direct mode terminates access immediately through a ciphertext update, motivated by patient consent withdrawal, with user-level and attribute-level granularity and an IND-CPA reduction under the q-BDHE assumption.

No audit element; attribute policy without a consent object; no multi-party approval; identity and authority only partially established; the proof concerns the static encryption predicate; scheme-level revocation is measured for cost, and enforcement at the consent object in a multi-institution exchange is not shown.

HealthDID, a DID-based EMR sharing system in which a zero-knowledge authorisation proof binds the data subject's commitment to a specific queryer's public key, separating authorisation from authentication, with three game-based definitions and three reduction theorems for anonymity, unforgeability and search privacy, and a reproducible performance evaluation with a public repository.

The theorems cover the identity and authority fragment only and no theorem states the conditions under which access is granted; no purpose, role or data-category policy; no time value is read by any algorithm; no revocation, withdrawal or states; multi-party denotes multiple stakeholders' privacy, not joint authorisation; no allow-and-deny suite, executed attacks or dataset, and self-scored feature tables.

12.caption: Security Properties Supported by the Proposed MVC-Based Consent Architecture
rows: DID and credential verification before a participant can contribute to the authorisation process
Designed to prevent unverified entities from being treated as legitimate participants.
Independent evaluation of identity and role or authority evidence
Designed to prevent successful authentication from being interpreted as unrestricted authorisation.
Threshold evaluation over independently verified approval participants
Designed to prevent a single participant from unilaterally activating sensitive healthcare data access when collective approval is required.
Evaluation of purpose and requested data scope against consent policy
Designed to prevent otherwise valid identities and approvals from being used to obtain data beyond the authorised scope.
Recording of verification results, approval evidence, policy evaluation, and final decisions
Designed to provide traceability and support accountability, auditing, and future verification.
The View submits requests while the Controller independently determines the security decision
Designed to prevent user-interface actions from being interpreted directly as trusted authorisation outcomes.
